Another Tik Horror

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
a cape flats father kills his tik addicted son

Unique Selling Point:
The horrors of tik addiction once again illustrated by a father killing his tik addicted son who attacked him. Father says it was in self defence. One person who is supporting him is another person who went through the horrors of a tik crazed son - Ellen Pakkies - who snapped and strangled him to death. We tell the story of another mother is the same area who is being terrorised by her tik addicted son who refuses to go for treatment. he is violent. he attacked his brother who ended up in hospital. We have asked the sister to take cell phone footage of him as he throws fit. We will interview the mother as the addict lies asleep inside the house. We may even ask the boy for an interview. . Treatment facilities are available in Cape Town so we ask how and why these addicts are not getting the treatment.? We show case two individuals who have managed to turn their lives around after treatment which provides hope to the story

Summary:
recently the wc cape govt released statistics of random testing of school children - 66% of school kids have used a drug. No wonder the metro police go on regular raids -and we join them. A top psychiatrist explains the science of tik addiction which causes psychosis and violence. He has treated hundreds of psychotic tik addicts. he will explain how difficult it is to try and get tik addicts into treatment. The program will also show how treatment centers run supportive groups to parents to empower them to deal with their children. Involuntary committals are an option - why is this not been used more?

Press Release:


Tik Horror
From violent bursts of anger, attacks on family members and serious destruction to property, living with a “Tik” or crystal methamphetamine addict can be a nightmare, but for any parent, killing your own child is an unthinkable act. For Sedick Abrahams however it became a reality when he stabbed his Tik addicted son to death during an altercation. His son Clinton had been using the drug for over a decade – which often triggered dangerous spikes of aggression towards his family. As one of the most addictive drugs in the world, it is tearing families apart and Abrahams isn’t the only parent who’s resorted to killing their child. Carte Blanche explores how this drug continues to destroy communities.


Script:


Tik addiction is destroying communities in the Western Cape and continues to tear families apart.

street name for crystal methamphetamine Tik is a central nervous stimulant and is one of the world’s most addictive drugs. It creates instant energy and euphoria, but can damage the frontal lobe of the brain, triggering spikes of aggression.

No-one knows it better than Cape Flats mother Maria Johnson. Her son started using tik three years ago and would continually steal from her home to pay for his next fix. He would often fly into a rage.

MARIA JOHNSON: one Sunday morning I was so upset I began to cry; I began to cry yes. My whole house was smashed.

Johnson says her son destroyed her home several times.

MARIA JOHNSON: I always tell people, it cost me R50 000 to make this place the place I want, the upstairs. Yoh its very heart sore, I can't stand it any more.

At her wits’ end, Johnson took out a restraining order…but her son simply ignored it. Two months ago he attacked his younger brother with a rock – the boy was admitted to hospital with serious injuries.

Eventually Johnson had her son arrested for theft.

Heart-breaking stories like these are a part of Joanie Frederiks’ daily work at Mitchell's Plain Impact Association

JOANIE FREDERICKS: It is as common as at least 2 people coming to me per week aside from the many WhatsApp’s that I am getting from people to say they don’t know what to do anymore. This is how bad it is and people when they say they have run out of options, they are speaking about killing them.

Johnson understands “those thoughts”.

MARIA JOHNSON: I have felt…when he’s asleep, that I could set him alight…really, I have felt like setting him alight in his sleep…the way he has carried on here.

Tik is rampant in Tafelsig Mitchell Plain. On this street lives Sedick and Mertyl Abrahams whose son also was addicted to tik.

Mertyl: He was a good child we really looked forward to good things he would do – play soccer, his sports…

Twenty-eight-year-old Clinton started using tik at the age of 14…. he also stole continually from the home and grew increasingly violent.

SEDICK ABRAHAMS: You see he used to throw my wife with boiling water, with the fish oil, he was throwing my wife and he was hitting her with the enamel pot and hitting her with the bottle and I just, what must I do? I was afraid I was living in fear because he can do anything to us.

His parents begged Clinton to find help but He refused. They felt helpless.

SEDICK ABRAHAMS: I was only praying me and my wife. That’s all we can do. Nothing else.

On the 31st of January this year there was yet another fight….

SEDICK: We were pushing with each other and I only grabbed the knife and the knife was fall on the floor and I kept the knife in front of him and he still keep on. So the knife just went into his chest.

As Clinton staggered from the house he bumped into his mother on her way home from work.
He came to me and said

Mertyl: "Mommy, my dad stabbed me..." Then he walked down the road and on the corner, at the stop street, he fell. Mertyl Abrahams:

Clinton died later that day from his injuries and Abrahams was arrested on a charge of murder.

One person who can truly empathize with Sedick is Ellen Pakkies. Her own story captivated the public imagination ten years ago. After years of torment and …after being physically attacked several times…she finally snapped and strangled her tik addicted son Adam in his sleep. She visited the Abrahams family.

ELLEN PAKKIES: Well you know I could sit there and just talk to him and give him hope because he was feeling very down. I mean down is not even the word because I don’t know really what he went through, because every one’s situation is different.

No one knows if Adam or Clinton were psychotic -- they were never assessed by doctors. Neuroscientist Dr Fleur Howells’s one special interest is in in tik and psychosis

DR FLEUR HSWELLS: So for people who regularly use methamphetamine. One in three is likely to develop a psychotic episode. One in three. So when an individual enters a psychotic state, what does occur is that the person is like a fearful animal. They are not able to cope in the environment that they find themselves in. So they will do anything to, for them, they perceive as survival. So they may be aggressive, they may break windows, but at the same time, its not from a malicious intent.

The devastating impact of tik is not unique to poorer areas. Erika de Kok knows all about the descent into insanity.

ERIKA DE KOK: I had an incredible life. A mother, 4 beautiful children, living this sort of suburban dream. Had a lovely career. In fact, one so much so that I was travelling locally, internationally on a regular basis.

Party recreational drug use and a personal tragedy led her to try out tik. Her life spiraled out of control. She lost her home, family and career. She ended up on the street.

ERIKA DE KOK: Its almost impossible for me to communicate the level of insanity that I was experiencing. So I would sometimes believe that I was in another reality and I would be talking to myself non stop while I walking through sandton with no shoes and I mean people thought that I was insane - which at that stage I absolutely was.

Last year drug testing at various schools in the western cape revealed that 67.7 percent of school children tested positive for drugs. Cape metro police have intensified their efforts to arrest dealers. There has also been an increase in the number of out patient rehabilitations centers.

LINK: Today we are in Mitchell’s plain where the city of cape town's matrix program is celebrating 10 years of existence, recognizing addicts and their families who have been through its program.

The matrix model of intensive out patient treatment is internationally recognized and there are now six such centers in the city’s clinics. Ismael Daniels is one of thousands of addicts who have been treated. He used tik from the age of 9. Life spiraled out of control but one incident changed his life.

ISMAEL: It came to a point where me and my, I am a twin brother you know, my twin bother is also here today, he is also in the recovery, it came to a point where we almost killed one other, you know for drugs. You know and I realized you know when he stabbed me in my face and I realized that you know, enough is enough.

Daniels has been clean now for 4 years.

ISMAEL: Yah you know this is an amazing feeling you know. You know like, I don’t know how I can explain the gratitude in words, but I am so grateful you know. Today, you know I know who I am and what I want from this life.

LINK: But what options do parents have whose children continue to use tik, who continue to be violent, who steal and still refuse to go for treatment?

Theses parents can approach matric centers for advise and support.

JP SMITH: You can contact the clinic and speak to someone or come in and go and see them at the clinics across the city who can all help you understand your legal powers, what opportunities there are for you. What role the criminal justice system plays in that and what to do in order to encourage your spouse, your child your parent, your friend to seek treatment and to get the constant back up to see that treatment through.

De Kok is now in a position to advises parents whose children refuse treatment. After two failed rehabilitation attempts, she managed to stop all drugs three years ago.

ERIKA DE KOK: The thing that just kept me going where my children and then at some point I thought, I just I can’t, I have to stay alive, I have to stay alive for them.

De Kok moved down to Cape Town with a suitcase and R500. She’s slowly rebuilding her life and mentoring recovering addicts – but her son had also developed a serious tik problem.

ERIKA DE KOK: I forced recovery on him, as a parent, because I would like to prevent him from having just a finger nail part of the experience that I had. I had to get a court order because he was underage, he was 18, and I forced it and it was the best thing that I did.

Her son is clean, and doing well now

In the meantime, the Abrahams’ are grappling with their loss.

Abrahams says he acted in self defense, but if a court finds him guilty of murder, he hopes for the same leniency shown toward Ellen Pakkies who received a community service sentence for killing her son.

With his wife at work, the father cut a lonely figure as he made his way into the Mitchells plain court, where a magistrate must consider his fate.

SEDICK: He is still my son; I mean we still love him in any case. Me and my wife we try to cope with each other, talk with each other, and that’s what’s happening all the time.
